claim: Serotonergic input has separable suppressive effects on the gain of ongoing and evoked visual activity.
source: Here, we show that serotonergic input has separable suppressive effects on the gain of ongoing and evoked visual activity.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including optogenetic stimulation, imaging, and pharmacological experiments.

claim: 5-HT1A receptors promote divisive suppression of spontaneous activity.
source: 5-HT1A receptors promote divisive suppression of spontaneous activity, while 5-HT2A receptors act divisively on visual response gain and largely account for normalization of population responses over a range of visual contrasts in awake and anesthetized states.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological blocking experiments with WAY-100135 (5-HT1A antagonist) shown in Figures 6 and 7, demonstrating that blocking 5-HT1A receptors abolishes suppression of spontaneous activity.

claim: 5-HT2A receptors act divisively on visual response gain.
source: 5-HT1A receptors promote divisive suppression of spontaneous activity, while 5-HT2A receptors act divisively on visual response gain and largely account for normalization of population responses over a range of visual contrasts in awake and anesthetized states.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological blocking experiments with MDL-100907 (5-HT2A antagonist) shown in Figures 6 and 7, demonstrating that blocking 5-HT2A receptors reduces suppression of evoked response magnitude.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) was combined with wide-field calcium imaging in mouse visual cortex.
source: We combined optogenetic stimulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) with wide-field calcium imaging, extracellular recordings, and iontophoresis of serotonin (5-HT) receptor antagonists in the mouse visual cortex.
evidence: The experimental methods are described in the abstract and detailed in the Materials and methods section, with results shown throughout the figures.

claim: Imbalanced 5-HT1A/2A activation may enhance internal broadcasts and reduce sensory drive.
source: Imbalanced 5-HT1A/2A activation, either through receptor-specific drug intake, genetically predisposed irregular 5-HT receptor density, or change in sensory bombardment may enhance internal broadcasts and reduce sensory drive and vice versa.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about the separable effects of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors on ongoing and evoked activity.

claim: Cortical states modulate ongoing activity and its interaction with sensory-evoked input.
source: Numerous studies have shown that cortical states modulate ongoing activity and its interaction with sensory-evoked input (Arieli et al., 1996; Deneux and Grinvald, 2016; Ferezou and Deneux, 2017; Ferezou et al., 2007; Fiser et al., 2010; Fox et al., 2006; Haider et al., 2007; He, 2013; Kasanetz et al., 2002; Kenet et al., 2003; Luczak et al., 2009; Markram et al., 1998; McGinley et al., 2015; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Raichle, 2015; Schölvinck et al., 2015; Shimaoka et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Neuromodulators can alter the balance between ongoing and evoked activity.
source: Neuromodulators that affect the state of cortical networks (Marder, 2012), however, can alter the balance between ongoing (partly top-down) and evoked (largely bottom-up) activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marder, 2012 and is part of the background knowledge establishing the rationale for the study.

claim: Serotonin is mainly released from 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe and median raphe nuclei.
source: One prominent neuromodulator involved in the modulation of the cortical state is serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) (Rapport et al., 1948), which is mainly released from 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe (DR) and median raphe (MR) nuclei (Dahlström and Fuxe, 1964; Descarries et al., 1982; Ishimura et al., 1988; Mengod et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The serotonergic system comprises widespread projections to all cortical and subcortical areas.
source: The serotonergic system comprises widespread projections to all cortical and subcortical areas (Hale and Lowry, 2011; Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992; Mengod et al., 2006; Vertes and Linley, 2007; Waterhouse et al., 1986)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Different 5-HT receptors are co-distributed across different cortical cell types.
source: The serotonergic system comprises widespread projections to all cortical and subcortical areas (Hale and Lowry, 2011; Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992; Mengod et al., 2006; Vertes and Linley, 2007; Waterhouse et al., 1986) with different 5-HT receptors (inhibitory or depolarizing) co-distributed across different cortical cell types (Hannon and Hoyer, 2008; Leysen, 2004; Santana et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus revealed its general modulatory influence on evoked cortical responses.
source: In the visual cortex, pioneering studies using electrical stimulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) revealed its general modulatory influence on evoked cortical responses (Gasanov et al., 1989; Moyanova and Dimov, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortical application of 5-HT or 5-HT receptor agonists showed either suppressive or facilitative effects.
source: Cortical application of 5-HT or 5-HT receptor agonists via microiontophoresis and single-cell recordings in vivo showed either suppressive or facilitative effects (Krnjević and Phillis, 1963; Reader, 1978; Watakabe et al., 2009; Waterhouse et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At the population level, 5-HT decreases mainly the gain of evoked responses without affecting spontaneous activity in awake monkeys.
source: Iontophoretic application of 5-HT into the visual cortex of awake monkeys in a recent study demonstrated that at the population level, however, 5-HT decreases mainly the gain of evoked responses without effecting spontaneous activity (Seillier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Seillier et al., 2017.

claim: Divisive scaling of evoked responses was attributed to selective activation of 5-HT2A receptors.
source: Such a distinct 5-HT effect on response gain was recently attributed to selective activation of 5-HT2A receptors (Zhang and Stackman, 2015) via several different approaches: after subcutaneous injection of a hallucinogenic 5-HT2A receptor agonist in mice (Michaiel et al., 2019), through whole-brain modelling (Deco et al., 2018) of human 5-HT2A receptor density and stimulation with lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and by direct and specific optogenetic activation of 5-HT2A receptors in the mouse visual cortex (Eickelbeck et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of 5-HT neurons in the mouse DRN showed 5-HT-induced divisive gain control of spontaneous firing without effect on stimulus-driven population responses in olfactory cortex.
source: Intriguingly, using optogenetic stimulation of 5-HT neurons in the mouse DRN (Dugué et al., 2014; Kapoor et al., 2016; Matias et al., 2017), only one study in olfactory cortex has shown so far a 5-HT-induced (divisive) gain control of spontaneous firing, without any effect on the gain of stimulus-driven population responses (Lottem et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lottem et al., 2016.

claim: DRN activation could separately reduce the weight of ongoing cortical activity relative to evoked activity.
source: This suggests that DRN activation could separately reduce the weight of ongoing cortical activity relative to evoked activity (Lottem et al., 2016), thereby possibly changing the balance of integration between internal priors (Berkes et al., 2011; Fiser et al., 2010) and external sensory input (Lottem et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited study by Lottem et al., 2016.

claim: ePet-Cre mouse line allows expression of Channelrhodopsin2 in 5-HT neurons.
source: To trigger the activation of 5-HT neurons in the DRN with precise timing, we used a transgenic ePet-Cre mouse line (Scott et al., 2005), which allows expression of Channelrhodopsin2 (ChR2) in 5-HT neurons by Cre-dependent expression of double-floxed adeno-associated virus (AAV, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citation to Scott et al., 2005 and described in the methods.

claim: Wide-field optical imaging of Ca2+ signals reflects suprathreshold population activity across upper cortical layers.
source: In order to simultaneously record activity of a large number of neurons across V1, we employed wide-field optical imaging of Ca2+ signals, shown to reflect suprathreshold population activity across upper cortical layers (Kim et al., 2016; Lütcke et al., 2013; Lütcke et al., 2010; Wallace et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: RCaMP was used to minimize interference with blue light employed to activate serotonergic neurons.
source: Specifically, we used the red-shifted fluorescent probe RCaMP (Akerboom et al., 2013; Dana et al., 2016; Figure 1a) to minimize interference with the blue light employed to activate serotonergic neurons in the DRN (Figure 1b) and to reduce light scattering caused by hemodynamic signals in comparison to GCaMP.
evidence: This is a methodological choice explained with citations and rationale.

claim: Photostimulation of the DRN suppresses neuronal responses in primary visual cortex (V1).
source: As control conditions we recorded evoked responses to visual stimuli (vertical grating with 100% contrast, presented 10 times at intervals of 3 s with 200 ms duration) and spontaneous activity over a total of 30 s (Figure 2ai, [V] and Figure 2aiii [S], respectively). In addition, we recorded the activity during these conditions with photostimulation (16 s train of 470 nm light pulses at 20 Hz and 50% duty cycle, marked as blue bars in Figure 2aii, [Vph] and Figure 2aiv, [Sph]) to activate 5-HT neurons in the DRN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, demonstrating suppression of both evoked and spontaneous activity during DRN photostimulation.

claim: After onset of photostimulation, a strong suppression of evoked visual responses is observed.
source: In contrast, after the onset of photostimulation, a strong suppression of evoked visual responses is observed, succeeded by a subsequent increase of the Ca2+ signal above pre-stimulation levels after cessation of photostimulation (Figure 2aii).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2aii.

claim: 5-HT-mediated suppression of cortical activity is present without external visual input.
source: Importantly, 5-HT-mediated suppression of cortical activity is present without external visual input; that is, following photostimulation, ongoing cortical activity rapidly declines below baseline levels (Figure 2aiv).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2aiv showing suppression of spontaneous activity.

claim: Suppression of spontaneous activity includes cortical areas beyond V1.
source: This suppression of spontaneous activity includes cortical areas beyond V1 (white contours in Figure 2b, 4th row; for assignment of cortical areas, see Figure 1aiv), suggesting 5-HT affects spontaneous drive through widespread ascending projections from the DRN across the entire cortex (Hale and Lowry, 2011).
evidence: This is observed in the imaging data shown in Figure 2b and supported by citation to Hale and Lowry, 2011.

claim: Suppression of spontaneous activity is significant 680 ms after the onset of DRN photostimulation.
source: The suppression is significant 680 ms (8 animals, p=0.04; paired t test with permutation correction) after the onset of DRN photostimulation, then it reaches a local minimum followed by an increase in activity (Figure 3ai).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3ai.

claim: The late increase of the RCaMP signal could indicate an increase of intracellular Ca2+ levels associated with 5-HT-receptor-mediated activation of the Gq/11 pathway.
source: This later elevation in the RCaMP signal could indicate an increase of intracellular Ca2+ levels (Eickelbeck et al., 2019) associated with the 5-HT-receptor-mediated activation of the Gq/11 pathway (Millan et al., 2008) and concomitant activation of store-operated channels (Celada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed RCaMP signal increase, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Spontaneous activity revealed by MUAs is significantly suppressed after 750±184 ms of DRN photostimulation.
source: Similar to RCaMP imaging, spontaneous activity revealed by MUAs is significantly (below two times standard deviation of pre-photostimulation activity) suppressed after 750±184 ms of DRN photostimulation in comparison to baseline spontaneous firing (Figure 3bi, light blue and stippled black line, respectively)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from MUA recordings shown in Figure 3bi.

claim: In contrast to the RCaMP signal, spiking activity is devoid of a subsequent elevation during photostimulation.
source: Note that in contrast to the RCaMP signal, spiking activity is devoid of a subsequent elevation. Instead, the suppression remains highly significant throughout photostimulation (−0.43±0.08; n=9 animals, p<0.001; one-sample t test; Figure 3bii, left bar).
evidence: This is observed by comparing RCaMP imaging data with MUA recordings, shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observed rise of the RCaMP signal may represent intracellular accumulation of Ca2+, rather than increase in spiking activity.
source: This further suggests that the observed rise of the RCaMP signal may represent intracellular accumulation of Ca2+, rather than increase in spiking activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing RCaMP and MUA data, where MUA shows no increase while RCaMP does.

claim: Augmented activity of 5-HT neurons via DRN photostimulation results in suppression of spontaneous activity in the visual cortex.
source: Altogether, it can be inferred that augmented activity of 5-HT neurons via DRN photostimulation results in suppression of spontaneous activity in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on spontaneous activity suppression.

claim: Suppression of spontaneous activity is divisive.
source: Additional analysis using linear regression shows that this suppression is divisive (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The amplitude of evoked activity declines toward negative values in the presence of DRN photostimulation.
source: While visually evoked responses of control conditions are characterized by repeated increase of the Ca2+ signal with a small adaptive decrease in the response amplitudes over time (Figure 5ai and 5bii, black trace), the amplitude of activity declines toward negative values in the presence of DRN photostimulation (Figure 5aii, dark blue trace).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5aii.

claim: Both the amplitude of the evoked responses and their baseline are reduced during DRN photostimulation.
source: Note that both the amplitude of the evoked responses and their baseline are reduced.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The evoked component is obtained by subtracting Sph from Vph.
source: To assess how much of the suppression in amplitude is due to the suppression of its baseline level, we subtracted image frames obtained under Sph conditions from those under Vph conditions (pixelwise and across single trials). The outcome (Figure 5aii, gray trace) is the photostimulation-induced suppression of the evoked response independent of suppression in spontaneous activity, that we refer to as the evoked component.
evidence: This is a methodological approach described and applied to the data shown in Figure 5aii.

claim: Amplitudes of evoked responses and evoked component are significantly lower than control during DRN photostimulation.
source: Following DRN photostimulation, amplitudes of evoked responses (Figure 5bi dark blue curve) and evoked component (Figure 5bi gray curve) are significantly lower than those of the control condition (Figure 5bi black curve; p<0.05; paired t test with permutation correction).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of the data shown in Figure 5bi.

claim: The time course of the baseline in the evoked responses during photostimulation is analogous to spontaneous activity during photostimulation.
source: Indeed, the time course of the baseline in the evoked responses during photostimulation is analogous to spontaneous activity during photostimulation (Figure 5bii, cf. dark blue and light blue traces, respectively)
evidence: This is observed by comparing the traces in Figure 5bii.

claim: The suppression of magnitude is highly significant as compared to control.
source: The suppression of magnitude is highly significant as compared to control (Figure 5biii, blue and black curves, respectively; p<0.05, paired t test with permutation correction).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of the data shown in Figure 5biii.

claim: In the photostimulated condition the magnitude of the evoked response resembles the evoked component.
source: Moreover, in the photostimulated condition the magnitude of the evoked response resembles the evoked component (Figure 5biii, cf. overlapping blue and gray curves, respectively; across all stimuli, #1:10, p>0.21, paired t test with permutation correction)
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 5biii with statistical confirmation.

claim: The suppression in response magnitude is separable from suppression of spontaneous activity.
source: Moreover, in the photostimulated condition the magnitude of the evoked response resembles the evoked component (Figure 5biii, cf. overlapping blue and gray curves, respectively; across all stimuli, #1:10, p>0.21, paired t test with permutation correction), confirming that the suppression in response magnitude is separable from suppression of spontaneous activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis shown in Figure 5biii.

claim: Extracellular recordings of MUA in V1 substantiate the observed suppressive effects on evoked responses at the spiking level.
source: Extracellular recordings of MUA in V1 substantiate the observed suppressive effects on evoked responses and their independence of baseline suppression at the spiking level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MUA recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 5-HT-induced reduction in the gain of evoked activity is independent of the reduction of ongoing activity.
source: This again demonstrates that 5-HT-induced reduction in the gain of evoked activity is independent of the reduction of ongoing activity and is well-captured by response magnitude in both recording methods.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing Ca2+ imaging and MUA data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Suppression of the evoked component is divisive.
source: Analogous to spontaneous activity, using linear regression, we found that the suppression of the evoked component is divisive (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing activity of 5-HT neurons in the DRN affects cortical activity in a divisive manner via two suppressive components.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that increasing activity of 5-HT neurons in the DRN affects cortical activity in a divisive manner via two suppressive components: one suppressing ongoing activity and another reducing the gain of visually evoked activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on both spontaneous and evoked activity.

claim: After blocking 5-HT2A receptors via MDL, the amplitude of the evoked response remains suppressed while its magnitude is only slightly reduced.
source: After blocking 5-HT2A receptors via microiontophoresis of MDL (see Methods) and parallel photostimulation of 5-HT neurons in the DRN, the amplitude of the evoked response remains suppressed, while its magnitude is only slightly reduced (Figure 6ai, blue).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data with MDL application shown in Figure 6ai.

claim: After subtraction of the spontaneous component during MDL treatment, the evoked component is nearly identical to control conditions.
source: Hence, after subtraction of the spontaneous component (Figure 6ai, light blue), the trace of the evoked component (Figure 6aii, gray) is nearly identical to control conditions (Figure 6aii, black) with no significant difference between magnitude values (Figure 6bi) except for a period immediately after onset of drug application (Figure 6bi, stimulus #2).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 6aii and quantified in Figure 6bi.

claim: The suppression of the baseline is preserved during MDL treatment.
source: In contrast, the suppression of the baseline is preserved (Figure 6bii, dark blue) and is similar to spontaneous activity during photostimulation and MDL treatment (Figure 6bii, light blue).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 6bii.

claim: The rising part of the RCaMP signal in the Sph condition during MDL application is significantly reduced compared to Sph without MDL treatment.
source: It is noteworthy that the rising part of the RCaMP signal in the Sph condition during MDL application (Figure 6bii, light blue, values #5:7) is significantly reduced as compared to Sph without MDL treatment (Figure 5bii, light blue; p=0.04, two-sample t test on the detrended traces).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing data with and without MDL treatment.

claim: Blocking 5-HT2A receptors reduces intracellular Ca2+ accumulation.
source: This suggests a reduction of the aforementioned intracellular Ca2+ accumulation (Eickelbeck et al., 2019) by effectively blocking 5-HT2A receptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed reduction in RCaMP signal rise during MDL treatment, supported by citation.

claim: Blocking of 5-HT1A receptors by WAY abolishes the suppression in spontaneous activity.
source: Conversely, blocking of 5-HT1A receptors by microiontophoresis of WAY (see Materials and methods) abolishes the suppression in spontaneous activity (Figure 6ci, light blue and Figure 6dii)
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data with WAY application shown in Figure 6ci and 6dii.

claim: The evoked component and magnitude of the response remain significantly suppressed during WAY application.
source: whereas the evoked component (Figure 6cii, gray) and hence, the magnitude of the response, remain significantly suppressed almost the entire time of drug application and photostimulation (Figure 6di, p<0.05, paired t test with permutation correction).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 6cii and 6di with statistical confirmation.

claim: Suppression of the response magnitude is significantly reduced via blocking 5-HT2A receptors.
source: Suppression of the response magnitude (Figure 7a, left two bars) is significantly (p<0.01, two-sample t test) reduced via blocking 5-HT2A receptors (−0.18±0.03 [blue] and −0.16±0.03 [gray], middle two bars, n=6 animals, p>0.05; one-sample t test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing conditions with and without MDL, shown in Figure 7a.

claim: No significant difference was found in magnitude of the evoked component by blocking 5-HT1A receptors.
source: No significant difference was found in magnitude of the evoked component by blocking 5-HT1A receptors (−0.36±0.05 [blue] and −0.37±0.05 [gray], right two bars; n=4 animals, p<0.001, one-sample t test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the WAY experiments shown in Figure 7a.

claim: 5-HT2A receptors dominantly contribute to the suppression of the evoked component by controlling the gain of the evoked response.
source: This suggests that 5-HT2A receptors dominantly contribute to the suppression of the evoked component by controlling the gain of the evoked response.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pharmacological blocking experiments with MDL shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Suppression of spontaneous activity is abolished via blocking of 5-HT1A receptors.
source: In contrast, suppression of spontaneous activity (Figure 7b, left blue bar) is abolished via blocking of 5-HT1A receptors (0.02±0.02, n=4 animals, p>0.5, one-sample t test; Figure 7b, right blue bar)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the WAY experiments shown in Figure 7b.

claim: No change in spontaneous activity suppression is seen by blocking 5-HT2A receptors.
source: while no such change is seen by blocking 5-HT2A receptors (−0.4±0.02, n=6 animals, p<0.01; one-sample t test; Figure 7b, middle blue bar).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MDL experiments shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Activation of 5-HT1A receptors dominantly contributes to suppression of spontaneous activity.
source: Thus, activation of 5-HT1A receptors dominantly contributes to suppression of spontaneous activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pharmacological blocking experiments with WAY shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors are major contributors to the suppression of activity in V1 induced by activation of 5-HT neurons in the DRN with separable impact on the gain of evoked and spontaneous components.
source: Together these results establish 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors as major contributors to the suppression of activity in V1 induced by activation of 5-HT neurons in the DRN with separable impact on the gain of evoked and spontaneous components.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the pharmacological blocking experiments.

claim: Visual responses progressively decline in amplitude with decreasing contrast.
source: As expected from earlier studies in mice (Porciatti et al., 1999), visual responses progressively decline in amplitude with decreasing contrast.
evidence: This is an expected result based on previous literature (Porciatti et al., 1999) and confirmed in the current data shown in Figure 8ai.

claim: Upon photostimulation of the DRN, overall amplitudes for each contrast are systematically suppressed.
source: Upon photostimulation of the DRN, we found that overall amplitudes for each contrast are systematically suppressed (Figure 8aii, dark blue traces), leading to a strong downward shift of the fitted tuning curve (Figure 8di, solid blue, R2=0.93).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 8aii and quantified in Figure 8di.

claim: There is a systematic increase in the latency and significant decrease in the duration of evoked response during DRN photostimulation.
source: Furthermore, we found a systematic increase in the latency and significant decrease in the duration of evoked response (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The suppressive spontaneous component contributes additively to the 5-HT-induced overall suppression of visual responses.
source: Above we showed that this suppressive spontaneous component contributes additively to the 5-HT-induced overall suppression of visual responses (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: At low contrast suppression is mainly due to the suppression in the spontaneous component.
source: This indicates that at low contrast suppression is mainly due to the suppression in the spontaneous component.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of magnitude suppression at different contrasts shown in Figure 8bi.

claim: The suppression at lower contrasts is similar to 5-HT-induced suppression of spontaneous activity.
source: Also note that the suppression at these lower contrasts is similar to 5-HT-induced suppression of spontaneous activity (Sph; −0.17±0.02, n=18 animals, p<0.001, one-sample t test; Figure 8bii).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 8bii.

claim: Fitting the Naka-Rushton function to the added values of evoked and spontaneous components reveals a close match to contrast tuning of control conditions.
source: Consequently, fitting the Naka-Rushton function to the added values of evoked and spontaneous components (Figure 8di, gray stippled curve; R2=0.93) reveals a close match to contrast tuning of control conditions (Figure 8di, solid black curve), indicating normalization across all contrasts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the curve fitting analysis shown in Figure 8di.

claim: In the anesthetized state, 5-HT-induced normalization of visual responses to different stimulus intensities is achieved by a linear combination of 5-HT-induced suppression of spontaneous and evoked components of cortical activity.
source: We conclude that in the anesthetized state, 5-HT-induced normalization of visual responses to different stimulus intensities is achieved by a linear combination of 5-HT-induced suppression of spontaneous and evoked components of cortical activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the contrast tuning experiments in anesthetized animals shown in Figure 8.

claim: During awake state the cortical 5-HT levels are increased.
source: Previous studies suggest that during awake state the cortical 5-HT levels are increased (Mukaida et al., 2007; Portas et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claim: 5-HT baseline levels may crucially affect the quantity of inducible suppression.
source: Because our results characterize 5-HT-induced suppression as divisive, both for spontaneous and evoked activity (Figure 4 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2, respectively), 5-HT baseline levels may crucially affect the quantity of inducible suppression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the divisive nature of suppression demonstrated in the data.

claim: Following DRN photostimulation cortical activity was suppressed in awake mice as compared to controls.
source: Figure 9a depicts the time traces of spatially averaged RCaMP signals across V1, evoked by different stimulus contrasts. As in anesthetized animals, following DRN photostimulation cortical activity was suppressed as compared to controls (Figure 9ai and aii, blue and black (control) traces, respectively).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data from awake mice shown in Figure 9a.

claim: In comparison to the anesthetized state, suppression at higher contrast is significantly reduced in awake mice.
source: In comparison to the anesthetized state, however, suppression at higher contrast (100%–25%) is significantly reduced (100%: p=0.010, 50%: p=0.012, 25%: p=0.019, 12%: p=0.392, 6%: p=0.694, n=5 animals, two-paired t test; Figure 9—figure supplement 1 shows the data derived from the same animals when they were anesthetized).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between awake and anesthetized states.

claim: In the awake state, the contrast-dependent decline in the magnitudes is not different between suppression of evoked activity and evoked component.
source: Importantly, in the awake state, the contrast-dependent decline in the magnitudes is not different between suppression of evoked activity and evoked component (Figure 9bi, blue and gray bars, respectively; p>0.31, paired t test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the awake experiments shown in Figure 9bi.

claim: In the awake state, normalization is largely controlled without the contribution of the spontaneous component.
source: This suggests that normalization is largely controlled without the contribution of the spontaneous component (Figure 9ci, blue (R2=0.98) and gray (R2=0.95) curves for evoked response and evoked component, respectively).
evidence: This is inferred from the curve fitting analysis shown in Figure 9ci.

claim: In the awake state, suppression of spontaneous activity constitutes an independent component with little influence on the magnitude and normalization of stimulus-evoked responses.
source: Thus, in the awake state, suppression of spontaneous activity (−0.11±0.3, n=5 animals, p=0.022, one-sample t test; Figure 9bii, left blue bar), even though similarly significant as in the anesthetized state (−0.17±0.04, n=5 animals, p=0.005, one-sample t test; Figure 9bii, right blue bar), constitutes an independent component with little influence on the magnitude and consequently, on normalization of stimulus-evoked responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing awake and anesthetized data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The 5-HT-induced gain is smaller in the awake than in the anesthetized state.
source: Second, we find that suppression of the magnitude is constant during photostimulation (Figure 5biii) and always lower in the awake (0.78±0.1, n=5) as compared to the anesthetized state (0.52±0.2, n=18, p<0.001, two-sample t test; Figure 8bi and Figure 9bi). Together, it is conclusive that the 5-HT-induced gain is smaller in the awake than in the anesthetized state (gaw<gan, Equation 5, second line).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing magnitude suppression between awake and anesthetized states.

claim: The weight of the baseline component is generally lower in the awake than in the anesthetized state.
source: Ultimately, Equation 5 implicates that the weight of the baseline component is generally lower in the awake than in the anesthetized state [(g×Sph)aw<(g×Sph)an].
evidence: This is a mathematical inference from the equations and data presented.

claim: In the awake state normalization is largely controlled by the gain of the evoked component.
source: This states that in the awake state normalization is largely controlled by the gain of the evoked component.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical analysis and experimental data comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: In contrast to the anesthetized state, under awake conditions normalization of cortical responses to different visual contrasts is largely conveyed by the gain of the evoked component.
source: In summary, in contrast to the anesthetized state, under awake conditions normalization of cortical responses to different visual contrasts is largely conveyed by the gain of the evoked component.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: There is a concurrent suppression of spontaneous activity constituting a separable component in the awake state.
source: Still, we find a concurrent suppression of spontaneous activity constituting a separable component, which has, in contrast to the anesthetized state, only minor additive effects on normalization of responses across varying stimulus intensities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the awake experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Activation of the serotonergic system impacts two entities of population activity in the visual cortex: internally ongoing (spontaneous) and visually driven (evoked) responses.
source: We show that activation of the serotonergic system impacts two entities of population activity in the visual cortex (V1): internally ongoing (spontaneous) and visually driven (evoked) responses, affecting both in a separable and divisive manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing all experimental findings.

claim: Each of these components is scaled through separate suppressive effects of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors.
source: Each of these components is scaled through separate suppressive effects of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors, respectively.
evidence: This is a main conclusion supported by the pharmacological blocking experiments.

claim: Application of 5-HT2A agonist caused suppression of neurons with strong responses and facilitation of those with weak responses in anesthetized monkey.
source: Previous studies in V1, using specific agonists for 5-HT1B and 5-HT2A receptors combined with single-unit recordings in anesthetized monkey, found a bi-directional modulation dependent on instantaneous firing levels. Application of 5-HT2A agonist caused suppression of neurons with strong responses and facilitation of those with weak responses, the opposite occurred when applying 5-HT1B receptor agonist (Shimegi et al., 2016; Watakabe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings from cited studies.

claim: Limitations associated with local iontophoretic 5-HT application could explain discrepancies with previous studies.
source: On the other hand, limitations associated with local iontophoretic 5-HT application, such as determining the exact onset of drug effects or the inevitable lack of cortical stimulation with layer- and cell type-specific synaptic weights of DRN synapses could be an alternative explanation.
evidence: This is speculation about methodological differences that could explain discrepancies with previous studies.

claim: Besides 5-HT neurons, subpopulations of glutamatergic cells in the raphe nuclei express ePet.
source: It should also be noted that besides 5-HT neurons, subpopulations of glutamatergic cells in the raphe nuclei express ePet (McDevitt et al., 2014; Sos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: ePet in non-serotonergic neurons is mainly observed in the median raphe nucleus.
source: ePet in non-serotonergic neurons is mainly observed in the median raphe nucleus (Pelosi et al., 2014; Sos et al., 2017), while in the dorsal and caudal nuclei (B6 and B7) only few neurons positive for ePet are non-serotonergic (Pelosi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Pharmacological blocking of 5-HT receptors in V1 largely diminished the induced suppressive effects.
source: However, as seen in our experiments pharmacological blocking of 5-HT receptors in V1 largely diminished the induced suppressive effects, contribution from other modulatory systems appears negligible for the present study.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological blocking experiments.

claim: Direct retinal projections to the DRN suggest its regulation well beyond the stimulation time window chosen in the study.
source: For instance, direct retinal projections to the DRN (Pickard et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016) suggest its regulation well beyond the stimulation time window chosen in our study.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies about retinal projections to the DRN.

claim: Slow periodic changes in 5-HT release occur naturally during day-night cycle.
source: In addition, slow periodic changes in 5-HT release occur naturally during day-night cycle (Portas et al., 2000; Tyree and de Lecea, 2017) and depend on seasonal factors (Spindelegger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Using the ePet-Cre mouse model and comparable photostimulation parameters, a consistent increase of DRN activity over 20 s of photostimulation was revealed.
source: Importantly, using the ePet-Cre mouse model and comparable photostimulation parameters as in our experiments (i.e. similar blue light intensity and frequency) to activate the DRN via fiber optics, a consistent increase of DRN activity in fMRI and MUA recordings over 20 s of photostimulation was revealed (Grandjean et al., 2019).
evidence: This is evidence from a cited study supporting the validity of the photostimulation approach used.

claim: Prolonged photostimulation of the DRN in SERT-Cre mice increased perceptual thresholds for tactile stimuli.
source: Prolonged (12 s) photostimulation of the DRN in SERT-Cre mice increased perceptual thresholds for tactile stimuli (Dugué et al., 2014)
evidence: This is evidence from a cited study showing behavioral relevance of DRN photostimulation.

claim: Wide-field recordings of RCaMP signals may also correlate with activity in the neuropil.
source: Wide-field recordings of RCaMP signals may also correlate with activity in the neuropil (Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a potential concern raised based on cited literature.

claim: MUA recordings largely reproduced the imaged suppressive effects, indicating that the observed reduction of RCaMP signals reflects reduced spiking output.
source: To rule out this possibility, we performed complementary recordings of MUA. These largely reproduced the imaged suppressive effects, indicating that the observed reduction of RCaMP signals indeed reflects reduced spiking output at the cortical population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing RCaMP imaging with MUA recordings.

claim: Autoreceptor-mediated suppression of 5-HT neurons within the DRN is an unlikely explanation for the late increase in RCaMP signal.
source: Autoreceptor-mediated suppression of 5-HT neurons within the DRN is an unlikely explanation for producing such late increase.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ accumulation of cortical neurons produces the late rise in the RCaMP signal.
source: We suggest that intracellular Ca2+ accumulation of cortical neurons produces the late rise in the RCaMP signal (Eickelbeck et al., 2019) due to 5-HT receptor-mediated activation of the Gq/11 pathway (Jang et al., 2012; Millan et al., 2008) with further activation of store-operated channels (Celada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on cited literature and the observed data.

claim: Ca2+ signals could increase through activation of 5-HT3 receptors.
source: Additionally, Ca2+ signals could increase through activation of 5-HT3 receptors (Nichols and Mollard, 1996) that are also capable of providing fast disynaptic inhibition via activation of interneurons (Varga et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a proposed alternative mechanism based on cited literature.

claim: In anesthetized animals, ongoing activity supplemented response normalization as a subtractive factor.
source: Using different stimulus intensities, we identified normalization of visual responses. In anesthetized animals, ongoing activity supplemented response normalization as a subtractive factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the contrast tuning experiments in anesthetized animals.

claim: The degree of 5-HT-controlled integration of sensory input and ongoing activity depends on cortical state and initial 5-HT levels.
source: Thus, the degree of 5-HT-controlled integration of sensory input and ongoing activity depends on cortical state and initial 5-HT levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: At the population level, suppression of ongoing activity may reflect an overall reduction of pyramidal cell spiking caused by hyperpolarization or by decrease in synaptic transmission.
source: At the population level, suppression of ongoing activity may reflect an overall reduction of pyramidal cell spiking caused by hyperpolarization or by decrease in synaptic transmission (Lőrincz and Adamantidis, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: Hyperpolarization of excitatory neurons was recently shown as an additional source of normalization processes.
source: In fact, hyperpolarization of excitatory neurons was recently shown as an additional source of normalization processes (Sato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Divisive scaling of evoked responses is most likely conveyed by predominant activation of excitatory 5-HT2A receptors.
source: In contrast, divisive scaling of evoked responses is most likely conveyed by predominant activation of (excitatory) 5-HT2A receptors, as suppression of the evoked component largely diminished after specific blocking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological blocking experiments with MDL.

claim: 5-HT2A receptors couple to the Gq/11 pathway leading to an increase in neuronal firing.
source: Moreover, 5-HT2A receptors couple to the Gq/11 pathway (Hannon and Hoyer, 2008) leading to an increase in neuronal firing rather than suppression.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Activation of GABAergic neurons may mediate reduction in activity of pyramidal neurons.
source: Therefore, activation of GABAergic neurons may mediate reduction in activity of pyramidal neurons (Gellman and Aghajanian, 1993).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on cited literature.

claim: Divisive modulation of visual cortical responses was shown to be specifically dependent on activation of soma-targeting parvalbumin expressing interneurons.
source: In fact, divisive modulation of visual cortical responses was shown to be specifically dependent on activation of soma-targeting parvalbumin expressing interneurons (Wilson et al., 2012, but see Lee et al. (2012) and Seybold et al., 2015) that dominantly express 5-HT2A receptors (Puig and Gulledge, 2011; Weber and Andrade, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Activation of 5-HT2A receptors may cause concomitant increase in depolarizing currents in pyramidal neurons, producing shunting inhibition.
source: Activation of 5-HT2A receptors may also cause concomitant increase in depolarizing currents in pyramidal neurons, producing shunting inhibition, which results in increased conductance.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on knowledge of receptor function.

claim: Shunting inhibition is known to affect the gain and the time constant of neuronal responses.
source: Such a mechanism is known to affect the gain and the time constant of neuronal responses (Carandini and Heeger, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Response duration declined during photostimulation of the DRN as compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, we find the duration of responses declined during photostimulation of the DRN as compared to controls.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reduction in response duration under the influence of 5-HT may indicate involvement of shunting inhibition in pyramidal neurons to effectively control response gain.
source: Thus, reduction in response duration under the influence of 5-HT may indicate involvement of shunting inhibition in pyramidal neurons to effectively control response gain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed reduction in response duration.

claim: Suprathreshold excitatory drive by 5-HT2A activation may be amplified by shaping the duration of 5-HT1A-mediated inhibition.
source: Suprathreshold excitatory drive by 5-HT2A activation may further be amplified by shaping the duration of 5-HT1A-mediated inhibition (Avesar and Gulledge, 2012; Stephens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on cited literature.

claim: 5-HT circuits modulate evoked visual population responses by partly plugging into the existing canonical machinery performing divisive normalization.
source: Altogether, we propose that 5-HT circuits modulate evoked visual population responses by partly plugging into the existing canonical machinery performing divisive normalization (Atallah et al., 2012; Carandini and Heeger, 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Selective activation of 5-HT2A receptors produced a strikingly consistent suppressive effect on the gain of visually evoked population responses.
source: In two recent studies, selective activation of 5-HT2A receptors produced a strikingly consistent suppressive effect on the gain of visually evoked population responses (Eickelbeck et al., 2019; Michaiel et al., 2019), despite cell-type and layer-specific differences across single cells (Michaiel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited recent studies.

claim: The distribution of a single neurotransmitter receptor density can account for a distinct function in sensory processing.
source: It also implicates that the distribution of a single neurotransmitter receptor density ('receptome') can account for a distinct function in sensory processing (Akimova et al., 2009; Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Deco et al., 2018; Goldberg and Finnerty, 1979; González-Maeso et al., 2007; Tauscher et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference supported by multiple citations.

claim: Joint action of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors unfold a separable and powerful scaling of ongoing and evoked components of population activity in V1.
source: In summary, joint action of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors unfold a separable and powerful scaling of ongoing and evoked components of population activity in V1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: A major difference observed in normalization between awake and anesthetized states is an overall stronger 5-HT-induced suppression of response gain in the anesthetized state.
source: A major difference that we observe in normalization between awake and anesthetized states is an overall stronger 5-HT-induced suppression of response gain in the anesthetized state
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing awake and anesthetized data.

claim: In the awake state response normalization is less dependent on ongoing activity and is possibly less influenced by internal cortical broadcasts.
source: which implicates that in the awake state response normalization is less dependent on ongoing activity and is possibly less influenced by internal cortical broadcasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings in awake animals.

claim: Ongoing activity contains top-down internal expectations, whereas evoked responses carry bottom-up signals about external sensory events.
source: Considering that ongoing activity contains (top-down) internal expectations, whereas evoked responses carry (bottom-up) signals about external sensory events
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Imbalance in the recruitment of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors affects integration of ongoing and evoked components, and thus, cortical information flow.
source: imbalance in the recruitment of these receptors (e.g. through specific agonist intake or disordered receptor expression pattern) affects integration of these components, and thus, cortical information flow.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Imbalance may lead to overemphasis of internally generated expectations relative to sensory input or vice versa.
source: This may either lead to overemphasis of internally generated expectations (i.e. favoring 'priors' Berkes et al., 2011; Fiser et al., 2010) relative to sensory input or vice versa (Lottem et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional consequences, supported by citations.

claim: Long-term malfunction of the interplay between ongoing and evoked activity facilitates psychiatric disorders like anxiety, depression and schizophrenia.
source: Long-term malfunction of such interplay facilitates psychiatric disorders like anxiety, depression and schizophrenia (Friston, 2005; Geyer and Vollenweider, 2008; Jardri et al., 2016; Lucki, 1998; Soubrié, 1986; Urban et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications, supported by multiple citations.

claim: This study may help to develop new ways of diagnosis and therapy by rebalancing of ongoing and evoked activity components.
source: Our study may help to develop new ways of diagnosis and therapy (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) by rebalancing of these components.
evidence: This is speculation about potential clinical applications of the findings.
